newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav opposition leader quits after 11 days.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav opposition leader quits after 11 days.

text.p: The leader of Yugoslavia's main opposition coalition resigned on Wednesday, just 11 days after taking up the post and less than a month before federal elections, Yugoslav media reported.
Former National Bank governor Dragomir Avramovic announced that he was stepping down as leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition for health reasons, independent BKTV said.
Quoting from Zajedno's statement, BK said Avramovic, who is 76 and has a history of health problems, was suffering from kidney trouble accentuated by higher blood pressure.

Analysts said the announcement would be a serious blow to Zajedno, which the most recent independent opinion poll said had overtaken the ruling coalition of Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic in popularity.

Avramovic told the Belgrade daily Nasa Borba in an interview to be published on Thursday: "If the coalition relies on me alone, that is not good, but I advised them they must stay together. I honestly wish they win the elections."

The latest poll, conducted by the weekly news magazine Vreme, said Avramovic had a 14-point lead over Milosevic as the country's most popular politician. It said Zajedno had 28 percent support, ahead of the ruling coalition with 24 percent.

Opinion polls in Yugoslavia are notoriously unreliable, but most analysts credited Avramovic with leading Zajedno to its unexpectedly strong position. As National Bank governor, he became a folk hero for halting hyperinflation two years ago.

He was sacked in May after losing a battle with government ministers over economic reform. His calls for fiscal discipline and free market measures threatened the political and economic monopoly enjoyed by Milosevic's Socialist Party.
When he accepted Zajedno's leadership, Avramovic told a news conference he agreed to the job because the current government was blocking desperately needed economic and political reform.
"I took it because I am convinced that the enormous changes that began here cannot be maintained in this essentially-feudal system," he said.
Analysts said Avramovic, a former World Bank economist, was the glue which held together the four parties comprising Zajedno after they had spent the previous seven months quarrelling.

"I reiterate I should be largely credited for rallying them and I know the voters will appreciate that," Avramovic told Nasa Borba. "I am left with undergoing treatment and watching the course of the upcoming elections calmly."
He said the coalition still had time to decide who would head Zajedno's list of candidates in the elections on November 3. "Understand me -- I can't" he added.

Few political observers expect Zajedno to win the elections in an environment where Milosevic's Socialists strictly control most media. But under Avramovic, it appeared to be well placed to seriously erode the ruling party's parliamentary power.
